name: Pari
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Andersen, Torben. 1988. Downstep in Pari: the tone system of a Western Nilotic language. Studies in African Linguistics 19(3): 261-315. OA PDF, journals.flvc.org/sal/article/download/107458/102778.
catalog_locator: abstract p.261; sec. 1 p.261-262; sec. 2 p.263; sec. 3.1 p.265
catalog_quote: Pari, a Western Ni10tic language, has a terraced-level tone system with total downstep. Although Pari could be analyzed as having three basic tone levels and automatic downstep, there is morphological evidence that it has two basic tone levels and non-automatic downstep. Furthermore, there is evidence that downstep is the manifestation of a floating high tone. ... In this article, I describe and analyze the tonal system of Pari. ... Pitch in Pari can be described abstractly in terms of a set of relative pitch level values. ... This sentence contains five vowels, each of which carries a level pitch. ... I shall mainly use nouns as examples, but verbs and other lexical word classes behave tonally in the same way as nouns.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all seven fragments of the deciding quotation are verbatim in the OA PDF we hold/txt at the stated pages (abstract p.261, sec.1 p.261-2, sec.2 p.263, sec.3.1 p.265), and the record's negative claim (zero occurrences of stress/accent/prominence) reproduces on the full text. (2) The classification 'tonal' (two levels H/L, non-automatic total downstep, every vowel bears a level pitch, lexical tonal classes) rests on the primary, fieldwork-based tone description by Torben Andersen, the only modern describer of Päri; Glottolog 5.1 lists no grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study, and the only grammar-type item (Simeoni 1978, missionary sketch) is said by Andersen to ignore tone. tone.quote: changes in vowel quality, segmental length and tone patterns, which are all abundantly documented in Western Nilotic ... Just as its moraic morphophonology, also Western Nilotic tone shows the side-by side of extending non-segmental material of the base by corresponding affix material, and complete overwriting – a point which I will develop here in full detail for verbal tone in Dinka (section 5.3) after a short discussion of the much simpler overwriting system of Jumjum (section 5.2).
